about.body1: ShrinkIt is a free online tool for resizing, compressing and converting images. It was built around one simple idea: your photos should never have to leave your device just to become smaller.
about.body2: Every operation — decoding, resizing, format conversion and download — happens locally in your browser using modern web APIs. There is no account, no upload queue and no server storing your files, because there is no server involved at all.

hero.title: Resize an Image
info1.p1: Every digital photo is a grid of tiny coloured dots called pixels. Your camera or phone decides how many dots fit in each row and column — a 4000×3000 photo holds 12 million of them, which is where the word “megapixel” comes from.
info1.p2: Each dot has to be stored somewhere, so more dots means more bytes. The file format matters too: JPG squeezes similar colours together to save space, while PNG keeps every dot exactly as it is — which is why the same picture can weigh 200 KB in one format and 2 MB in another.
info1.p3: When a site talks about “file size”, it simply means this storage weight, usually shown in kilobytes (KB) or megabytes (MB).
info1.title: What is an image file size?
info2.p1: There are two levers, and they do different things. Resizing changes the dot grid itself — shrinking a photo from 4000×3000 to 1900×1100 throws away roughly three quarters of the pixels, so the file gets dramatically smaller without looking any different at normal viewing sizes.
info2.p2: Compression keeps the grid but stores it more cleverly. With JPG you pick a quality level: 90% looks identical to the original for most photos, while 60% can halve the file size again with only tiny artefacts if you look very closely.
info2.p3: The practical recipe: first resize to the dimensions you actually need — about 1900×1100 is plenty for the web — then save as JPG at around 90% quality. That is exactly what this tool does in one click, and your images never leave your device while it happens.
info2.title: How can I reduce my image's file size?
privacy.intro: This page explains in plain language what happens to your images when you use ShrinkIt.
privacy.s1d: When you add an image, it is read into your browser's memory. Decoding, resizing, format conversion and the download are all performed locally on your device using standard web APIs (Canvas, Web Workers). At no point is your image transmitted to ShrinkIt or to any third party, because there is no server component to send it to.
privacy.s1t: 1. Your images never leave your device
privacy.s2d: ShrinkIt strips metadata (EXIF) from processed images by default, which removes things like camera model, GPS coordinates and timestamps. You can optionally keep the original metadata with the “Keep photo metadata (EXIF)” switch; even then, the data stays inside the file you download — it is never sent anywhere.
privacy.s3d: This site uses no analytics, no advertising trackers and no cookies for tracking. If you install ShrinkIt as an app, its offline cache also lives only on your device.
privacy.s4d: Because everything runs locally, closing the tab ends the story: there is no account to delete and no server copy to request. If you have questions about this policy, reach out via the contact page.
privacy.s4t: 4. Nothing to delete, because nothing is stored

settings.background_tip: Used when the original image has transparency but the output format does not (e.g. PNG → JPG).
settings.format_tip: JPG is best for photos; PNG keeps transparency; WebP is the modern lightweight choice; GIF suits simple graphics.
settings.lock_tip: Keeps width and height proportional while you resize.
settings.mode_crop_tip: Trims the edges to match the target proportions, then resizes — no distortion.
settings.mode_fit_tip: Fits the whole image inside the target size, keeping proportions; the rest is filled with the background colour.
settings.mode_stretch_tip: Resizes directly to the exact dimensions, even if the proportions change.
settings.preserve_exif_hint: Off by default: camera and location data are stripped for privacy.
settings.resolution_tip: Dots per inch — written into JPG/PNG metadata and used to convert cm/inches to pixels.
